title: Water and salt: ADH, renin and aldosterone
goal: Explain how vasopressin (ADH) and the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system respond to exercise, how training expands plasma volume, and why ADH that stays high can turn overdrinking into hyponatraemia in long events.

steps.title: Shrinking plasma, two regulators
steps.text:
Hard exercise shrinks [plasma volume](g:plasma-volume): water moves into working muscle and leaves as sweat. In 15 men cycling, it fell 3.7% at 100 W, 8.8% at 175 W and 12.4% at 225 W [[c:efl-pv-fall]]. Plasma loses more water than salt, so it gets more concentrated: its [osmolality](g:osmolality) rises.

Two hormone systems defend water and salt:

| | [vasopressin (ADH)](g:vasopressin) | [aldosterone](g:aldosterone) |
|---|---|---|
| released from | back of the pituitary (peptide) | adrenal cortex (steroid) |
| main trigger | rising osmolality | angiotensin II |
| at the kidney | keeps water | keeps sodium, so water follows |
| acts within | minutes | hours |

The heat module covers sweat itself; this lesson is about the hormones.

claims.text: Plasma volume falls during exercise, more at higher intensities (about −4%, −9% and −12% at 100, 175 and 225 W of cycling).

evidence.quote: The % delta PV was -3.7%* at 100 W, -8.8%* at 175 W, and -12.4%* at 225 W.
Bouts of acute exercise have been shown to produce a transient haemoconcentration immediately after long distance running, bicycle ergometry and both maximal and submaximal swimming exercise.

steps.title: ADH: set by salt, nudged by stress
steps.text:
In graded cycling, plasma sodium, osmolality and ADH rose only once intensity passed about 40% VO₂max, and ADH tracked osmolality closely [[c:efl-adh-osm]]. That is ADH doing its main job: when plasma gets saltier, keep water.

But ADH has other triggers. In 82 runners of a 56 km ultramarathon, ADH rose almost fourfold although plasma sodium was unchanged [[c:efl-adh-nonosm]]. Such non-osmotic triggers are thought to include nausea, pain, low blood glucose and inflammatory signals; IL-6, a signal released by working muscle, rose 12.5-fold in the same runners.

Why it matters: ADH that stays up when plasma is *not* concentrated tells the kidney to keep water it should be getting rid of.

claims.text: In graded cycling, plasma sodium, osmolality and ADH rose curvilinearly and significantly only above about 40% VO₂max, with ADH closely correlated with osmolality.

evidence.quote: Plasma Na+ concentration, Osm, and AVP increase were curvilinear with graded exercise and were significant only when work intensity exceeded 40% VO2max.

However, delta AVP was significantly correlated with delta Na+ (r = 0.86*) and delta Osm (r = 0.83*), whereas delta PRA had low correlations with delta Na+ (r = 0.33, NS), delta Osm (r = 0.29, NS), and delta AVP (r = 0.43, NS).

claims.text: After a 56 km ultramarathon, ADH was markedly raised (3.9-fold) although plasma sodium was unchanged, pointing to non-osmotic stimuli.

evidence.quote: Increases in the plasma (AVP)(p) (3.9-fold), oxytocin (1.9-fold), brain natriuretic peptide (4.5-fold), and IL-6 (12.5-fold) were highly significant (P < 0.0001).
(AVP)(p) was markedly elevated after the ultramarathon despite unchanged plasma [Na(+)](.)

steps.title: Renin, angiotensin, aldosterone: the sodium keeper
steps.text:
The [renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system](g:renin-angiotensin) is a chain:

1. The kidney releases **renin** when sympathetic drive rises and its own blood flow falls.
2. Renin turns angiotensinogen from the liver into angiotensin I, which becomes **angiotensin II**: it narrows blood vessels and triggers thirst.
3. Angiotensin II releases **aldosterone**, which makes the kidney keep sodium; water follows the sodium.

In graded cycling, renin activity rose in a straight line with workload, even at easy loads, and tracked sympathetic drive rather than osmolality [[c:efl-renin]]. So ADH answers "is the plasma too salty?", while renin answers "is the body under strain?"

Aldosterone is a steroid, so its sodium-keeping lasts well beyond the session.

claims.text: Plasma renin activity rose linearly with exercise intensity, significantly at all workloads, behaving as a general stress response to sympathetic activity rather than to osmolality.

evidence.quote: PRA increase was linear and significant at all work levels.
c) the stimulation of the renin-angiotensin system is a more general stress response, which responds to increasing sympathetic nervous activity.

steps.title: Bigger plasma volume, and the overdrinking trap
steps.text:
**Training.** Repeated sessions expand plasma volume. In 8 trained men, 2 h a day of cycling at 65% VO₂max for 8 days raised it by 427 mL (12%); renin and ADH rose about ninefold during each session, helping keep sodium and water [[c:efl-hypervol]]. Over weeks, the kidney keeps more sodium through a more sensitive aldosterone action [[c:efl-aldo]]. A bigger plasma volume helps [stroke volume](g:stroke-volume) and heat loss, and dilutes [haemoglobin](g:haemoglobin) concentration.

**Long events.** [Exercise-associated hyponatraemia](g:hyponatraemia) is caused mainly by drinking more than the kidneys can excrete. ADH that stays up for non-osmotic reasons makes that easier, because the kidney keeps the extra water [[c:efl-eah]]. How much and what to drink is the hydration module's job.

claims.text: Eight days of 2 h daily cycling at 65% VO₂max expanded plasma volume by 427 mL (12%), associated with a ninefold rise in renin activity and ADH during exercise.

evidence.quote: After training, BV increased by 457 ml (+8.1% P less than 0.05), due to an increase in PV of 427 ml (+12.1%, P less than 0.05); red cell volume was essentially constant (delta = +30 ml, NS).

Plasma hypervolemia during training was associated with two major factors: 1) a ninefold elevation in PRA and AVP during exercise that facilitated Na+ and H2O retention, and 2) a progressive, chronic increase in plasma albumin content that provided increased H2O-binding capacity for the blood.

claims.text: Endurance training expands plasma volume, with reduced urine output from greater renal sodium reabsorption through a more sensitive aldosterone action.

evidence.quote: The mechanism of reduced urine output appears to be increased renal tubular reabsorption of sodium through a more sensitive aldosterone action in man.
Expansion of blood volume (hypervolemia) has been well documented in both cross-sectional and longitudinal studies as a consequence of endurance exercise training.

claims.text: The primary cause of exercise-associated hyponatraemia is drinking beyond the kidneys' ability to excrete water; failure to suppress ADH, from non-osmotic stimuli, may contribute.

evidence.quote: Although the primary cause of exercise-associated hyponatremia (EAH) is relative overconsumption of fluids beyond the kidneys' ability to excrete excess fluid, the mechanisms limiting maximum renal excretory ability during exercise remain to be elucidated.

Therefore, an inability to maximally suppress (AVP)(P) during exercise as a result of nonosmotic stimulation of AVP secretion may contribute to the pathogenesis of exercise-associated hyponatremia if voluntary fluid intake were to exceed fluid output.

points: Hard exercise shrinks plasma volume and concentrates the plasma; ADH (keeps water) and aldosterone (keeps sodium) defend it.
ADH follows osmolality above about 40% VO₂max, but other triggers (thought to include nausea, pain and the stress of the effort) can keep it high even when sodium is normal.
Renin rises with workload as a stress response to sympathetic drive; angiotensin II then releases aldosterone.
Training expands plasma volume through these hormones; in long events, ADH that stays high makes overdrinking more likely to cause hyponatraemia.

variants.stem: During a hot 2 h ride, a cyclist's vasopressin (ADH) rises. What does it do at the kidney?

options.text: Makes it keep water, so less urine is made
options.why: Right: ADH is the antidiuretic hormone; it lets the kidney take water back into the blood.

options.text: Makes it keep sodium, so water follows
options.why: That is aldosterone's job. ADH acts on water directly.

options.text: Makes it release renin, to raise blood pressure
options.why: Renin release is driven mainly by sympathetic nerves and low kidney blood flow, not by ADH.

options.text: Makes it excrete more water, to cool the body
options.why: The opposite: ADH reduces urine; cooling comes from sweat, not urine.

variants.stem: A marathoner's ADH is high at the finish. What is the hormone telling her kidneys to do?

options.text: Hold on to water and make less urine
options.why: Right: ADH makes the kidney return water to the blood.

options.text: Hold on to sodium and lose potassium
options.why: That is aldosterone, the steroid from the adrenal cortex.

options.text: Get rid of water and make more urine
options.why: This is the opposite of ADH's action; low ADH lets the kidney dump water.

options.text: Make glucose to keep blood sugar up
options.why: The kidney can make some glucose, but that isn't ADH's job; ADH controls water.

variants.stem: During a hard ride, a cyclist's plasma osmolality rises although she hasn't eaten any salt. Why?

options.text: Plasma loses more water than salt, so what is left is more concentrated
options.why: Right: water moves into muscle and out as sweat, which is more dilute than plasma.

options.text: Working muscles release extra sodium into the blood
options.why: Muscle releases potassium in hard work, but the main cause is water loss from the plasma.

options.text: ADH adds salt to the blood
options.why: ADH keeps water; it doesn't add salt. Rising osmolality is its trigger, not its result.

options.text: Sweat removes more salt than water from the plasma
options.why: The reverse: sweat is usually more dilute than plasma, so it takes more water than salt.

variants.stem: A runner does 30 min at 30% VO₂max one day and 30 min at 70% VO₂max another day, in cool conditions. Where should you expect a clear rise in ADH?

options.text: Only at 70%, once osmolality rises
options.why: Right: ADH and osmolality rose significantly only above about 40% VO₂max.

options.text: Equally in both, as any run raises ADH
options.why: ADH follows osmolality, which barely changes in easy exercise.

options.text: Only at 30%, since slow runs last longer
options.why: Both runs last 30 min here; the harder one concentrates plasma more.

options.text: In neither, as ADH only rises with dehydration
options.why: Dehydration raises it more, but hard exercise alone concentrates plasma enough to raise ADH.

variants.stem: At the finish of a 56 km ultramarathon, a runner's plasma sodium is normal, yet her ADH is about four times the pre-race value. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Non-osmotic triggers such as nausea, pain or stress are driving ADH
options.why: Right: with sodium unchanged, the rise must come from triggers other than osmolality.

options.text: Her plasma must be very concentrated
options.why: Normal sodium means plasma osmolality is roughly normal; the rise isn't osmotic.

options.text: The ADH test is wrong, since ADH only follows sodium
options.why: ADH mainly follows osmolality, but other stimuli raise it too; a high value with normal sodium is real.

options.text: She drank too little, so her blood volume is huge
options.why: Drinking too little would shrink, not enlarge, blood volume, and would usually raise sodium.

variants.stem: In the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone chain, which hormone directly tells the kidney to keep sodium?

options.text: Aldosterone
options.why: Right: aldosterone, a steroid from the adrenal cortex, makes the kidney reabsorb sodium.

options.text: Renin
options.why: Renin is the enzyme that starts the chain; it doesn't act on sodium handling itself.

options.text: Vasopressin (ADH)
options.why: ADH makes the kidney keep water, not sodium.

options.text: Angiotensinogen
options.why: This is the inactive precursor from the liver that renin acts on.

variants.stem: In a ramp test on a cool day, a cyclist's renin activity climbs with every step, even the easy ones, while plasma sodium hasn't changed yet. Why?

options.text: Rising sympathetic drive to the kidney releases renin
options.why: Right: renin tracked workload and sympathetic activity, not osmolality.

options.text: Renin responds to salty plasma, like ADH
options.why: That is ADH's trigger; renin barely correlated with sodium or osmolality.

options.text: Aldosterone rises first and releases renin
options.why: The order is the other way round: renin leads to angiotensin II, which releases aldosterone.

options.text: The cyclist is already badly dehydrated
options.why: Early in a ramp test there is little fluid loss; the rise comes from sympathetic drive.

variants.stem: During a hard 1 h ride, a cyclist's aldosterone rises from 200 to 500 pmol·L⁻¹ (+150%), while plasma volume falls 12%. By how much did the amount of aldosterone in the plasma change?

options.why: This is the raw concentration change, with no correction for the smaller plasma volume.
This multiplies by 1.12 instead of 0.88: the correction goes the wrong way.
This subtracts percentages (150 − 12). Volumes multiply: 2.5 × 0.88 = 2.2.

variants.solution: Amount = concentration × volume. Before: 200 × 1 = 200. After: 500 × 0.88 = 440. 440 ÷ 200 = 2.2, so +120%.

variants.stem: During a hilly half marathon, a runner's ADH rises from 2.0 to 5.0 pg·mL⁻¹ (+150%), while plasma volume falls 10%. By how much did the amount of ADH in the plasma change?

options.why: This is the raw concentration change, with no correction for the smaller plasma volume.
This multiplies by 1.10 instead of 0.90: the correction goes the wrong way.
This subtracts percentages (150 − 10). Volumes multiply: 2.5 × 0.90 = 2.25.

variants.solution: Amount = concentration × volume. Before: 2.0 × 1 = 2.0. After: 5.0 × 0.90 = 4.5. 4.5 ÷ 2.0 = 2.25, so +125%.

variants.stem: After the bike leg of an Olympic-distance triathlon, an athlete's renin activity rises from 1.0 to 4.0 units (+300%), while plasma volume falls 15%. By how much did the amount of renin in the plasma change?

options.why: This is the raw concentration change, with no correction for the smaller plasma volume.
This multiplies by 1.15 instead of 0.85: the correction goes the wrong way.
This subtracts percentages (300 − 15). Volumes multiply: 4.0 × 0.85 = 3.4.

variants.solution: Amount = concentration × volume. Before: 1.0 × 1 = 1.0. After: 4.0 × 0.85 = 3.4. 3.4 ÷ 1.0 = 3.4, so +240%.

variants.stem: After a 10-day training camp, a healthy cyclist's haemoglobin concentration is 6% lower than before. He feels fine and rides well. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: His plasma volume has expanded, diluting the same red cells
options.why: Right: in the first weeks of training, plasma expands while red cell volume barely changes.

options.text: He has lost red cells and is becoming anaemic
options.why: Possible but unlikely in a fit, well rider after a camp; dilution by a bigger plasma volume fits better.

options.text: Training has slowed down his red cell production
options.why: Training doesn't suppress red cell production; red cell mass, if anything, rises over months.

options.text: He is dehydrated, which lowers haemoglobin
options.why: Dehydration shrinks plasma and raises haemoglobin concentration, the opposite.

variants.stem: A slow marathoner drinks a cup of water at every station for 5 h and finishes 1.5 kg heavier, confused, with a blood sodium of 128 mmol·L⁻¹. What is the main cause?

options.text: She drank more than her kidneys could excrete while ADH stayed up
options.why: Right: weight gain shows fluid overload; ADH kept the kidney holding on to the extra water.

options.text: She lost too much sodium in sweat
options.why: Sweat sodium losses can add to it, but gaining weight shows the main problem is excess water.

options.text: She is dehydrated, which concentrates the blood
options.why: She gained weight, and dehydration raises, not lowers, blood sodium.

options.text: Her ADH was too low to hold sodium
options.why: ADH keeps water, not sodium; a high, not low, ADH makes overdrinking dangerous.

variants.stem: In 82 ultramarathoners who drank as they wished, ADH rose almost fourfold with plasma sodium unchanged, and the authors suggest non-osmotic ADH may contribute to hyponatraemia. What most limits that conclusion?

options.text: Sodium stayed normal, so the link to hyponatraemia is inferred, not observed
options.why: Right: an observational study with fluid balance maintained; it shows high ADH, not that it caused hyponatraemia.

options.text: 82 runners are too few to measure a hormone change
options.why: 82 is a good sample for a 3.9-fold change; the limit is the design, not the size.

options.text: ADH can't be measured reliably in plasma
options.why: Plasma ADH is measured routinely; the issue is what the data can show, not the assay.

options.text: A 56 km race is too long for hormones to change
options.why: Hormones changed strongly; long races are exactly where hyponatraemia occurs.
